A 51 y.o African-American man with schizoaffective disorder, depressive and post-traumatic stress disorder was referred to a community mental health center to address medication non-adherence and lack of medication effectiveness. Within 4-weeks of this dosing strategy, auditory hallucinations returned and worsened. Oral aripiprazole dose increased to 7.5 mg/day with improvement in symptoms but at 2-week and 3 week follow-ups auditory hallucinations returned so aripiprazole LAI frequency increased to every 3-weeks (and 7.5 mg/day oral). Pharmacogenetic testing revealed the patient to carry the rs1799732 (-141C/ Del) variant (without complement to the + chromosomal strand) and he was switched to 882 mg/3 weeks of injectable aripiprazole lauroxil without oral aripiprazole in December of 2015 and as of February 2017 continues to tolerate the aripiprazole lauroxil and reports not needing oral aripiprazole.

Case report. Variant referred to in the paper as c.85T>C. A 35-year-old man with stage IIIB rectal adenocarcinoma received 5-fluorouracil concurrent with pelvic radiation followed by surgery with colostomy. The patient was then started on mFOLFOX-6 but was admitted the same evening due to cardiomyopathy. FOLFOX was discontinued and IROX was started. Follow-up showed complete cardiac function recovery. The patient was found to be heterozygous for the c.85T>C variant, "resulting in reduced DPYD enzymatic activity and potentially increased risk of 5-FU toxicity" according to the authors. However, it should be noted that the patient also carried the TYMS 2R/2R genotype which predicts low TYMS expression, which the authors state "also increases the risk for 5-FU toxicity" and that the c.85T>C variant has been assigned a normal function by CPIC. The patient's brother died while receiving 5-FU-containing chemotherapy for advanced gastric cancer.

Case report. A female patient with breast cancer was treated with tamoxifen, 3-amino-1-hydroprolylildene bisphosphonate and 5-fluorouracil. She developed severe toxicity in 2 weeks of treatment, and 5-fluorouracil treatment was stopped. Toxicity was diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, leukopenia. Analysis of DPD cDNA showed heterozygosity for a 165bp deletion that results from exon skipping. Sequence analysis of the genomic region encompassing the skipped exon showed that the patient was heterozygous for a G to A point mutation in the invariant GT splice donor sequence in the intron downstream of the skipped exon. This variant is now referred to as DPYD*2A. DPD activity in leukocytes (3.1 nmol/mg/h) was decreased compared to mean activity of DPD in controls (9.6+/-3.7), and comparable to that observed for obligate heterozygotes.

The rs118192172 T allele was reported in a German pedigree where the proband died of a fulminant malignant hyperthermia (MH) episode after exposure of halothane during general anesthesia. Family members of the proband underwent in vitro contracture test (IVCT) screening as well as genetic testing of RYR1. However, the T allele segregated with the MH Susceptible (MHS) phenotype on one branch of the pedigree, which included the proband, but not the other, where it was not discovered. On the branch of the pedigree that included the proband, the T allele segregated with the MHS phenotype but as a part of two distinct haplotypes. The sister of the proband inherited a TT genotype for each haplotype associated with the T allele. Severity of the her MHS phenotype was not different as compared to the phenotype associated with the CT genotype. The mother, sister, and two sons of the proband had the T allele and the MHS phenotype. One daughter of the proband that carried the haplotype carrying the causative mutation, tested as MH negative (MHN) demonstrating possible discordance between phenotype and genotype. On the other branch of the pedigree, a father and his two sons did not carry either haplotype associated with the T allele and all three were diagnosed as MHS via IVCT. A 70 year old many underwent surgery for and had before never been administered volatile anesthetics. Anesthesia was induced with 1 mg midazolam (0.014 mg/kg) and 100 mg propofol (1.4 mg/kg). Rocuronium, 50 mg (0.71 mg/kg), was used to facilitate tracheal intubation (without complication). Anesthesia continued with isoflurane (end-tidal 0.43–1.0 vol%) and intermittent doses of fentanyl, rocuronium, and hydromorphone. Heart rate was controlled with metoprolol. Ciprofloxacin and metronidazole were given before incision. Approximately 5 hours after surgery the patient began to develop symptoms of malignant hyperthermia (MH). Dantrolene was administered and the patient had to go to the ICU for several days, then back to the hospital. The patient recovered and one daughter explained that she had experienced muscle stiffness after succinylcholine and was told that she had an MH episode but never underwent contracture testing. Her father (the proband), her mother, and herself were tested for 17 known RYR1 mutations.
